4. The case of the Ministry of Energy is, that on the appellant's application before the respondent for absorbing him as Director of the BOGMC the then President's Secretariat (since dissolved) requested the Ministry of Establishment (respondent No.2) to take steps in the matter. Respondent No. 2 by its letter dated 24 December 1989 requested respondent No.1 to take necessary steps commenting that it was not required to have any role in the matter. After obtaining the opinion of BOGMC the President's Secretariat was informed that the appellant could not be appointed as a Director on permanent basis and that his prayer cannot be considered because there was no such provision in the Rules of the Corporation though there was scope for absorption in the civilian post according to Martial Law Orders Nos. 103, 132 and 135. After the specified period of his contract the appellant could be appointed in the vacant post of General Manager of the Corporation by the Chairman of the Corporation subject to the fulfillment of the conditions of the Rules of the Corporation. The Corporation, respondent No.3, informed respondent No. 1 that the appellant was at that time working as a Director and, as such, it would not be reasonable to appoint him, one step below, in the post of General Manager and that he would be the junior most General Manager and there might be administrative complexities for absorbing him in that post of Director. The administrative Ministry might absorb the appellant as a Director through proper committee on the basis of the power conferred by the Ministry of Establishment. The matter was placed before the Departmental Promotion and Appointment Board of respondent No. 1 for consultation. The Board recommended that the appellant be absorbed in the post of Director as a regular incumbent after cancelling his contract. With the approval of the then President of Bangladesh, the appellant was absorbed as a regular incumbent with effect from 1 January, 1989. When on 29 December, 1990 the Ministry of Establishment wanted to know from respondent No. 1 on what basis the appellant was absorbed as a regular incumbent it got revealed that it was done violating the prevailing government rules and procedure. The Departmental Promotion and Appointment Board had no power to recommend for the appointment of a Member of Board of Directors of a corporation as regular incumbent and the recommendation made by the said Board in respect of the appellant was without jurisdiction. For the cancellation of the appointment a summary was sent by respondent No. 1 to the President's Secretariat of the Acting President from where the same was sent to the Ministry of Establishment and the Ministry of Law for their opinion. The Ministry of Establishment opined that the Government reserved the power of the appointment of the Chairman/ Managing Director/Member/Director of the Autonomous Organization and that the absorption of the appellant as regular incumbent in the post of Director was liable to be cancelled. The Ministry of Law and Justice also opined that the appointment in the post of Director of the Corporation was beyond the jurisdiction of the Departmental Board of Promotion and Appointment. Accordingly, with the approval of the Acting President the appointment was cancelled. The appellant continued in the same contractual position without any fresh joining report and he was allowed to continue till 31 December, 1991 and he continued as such without taking the matter to the court till 15 December, 1991. Meanwhile he prayed for continuation of his service on further contract basis. 

 12. In 1982 the Martial Law was imposed on the country with a bang and a much-heralded claim that the armed forces of the country should have a participatory role and a share in the administration of the country. On 27 January, 1983 the Defence Services Officers (Appointment and Fixation of Seniority in Civil Post) Rules 1983, was made. These Rules did not, as such, provide for absorption of defence personnel in civil administration. Thereafter, the Chief Martial Law Administrator passed one after another three Orders, Martial Law Orders Nos. 103, 132 and 135 for inducting army personnel and for their absorption in the civilian administration. Paragraph 2 of Martial Law Order No. 103 provided, subject to certain provisions: 

 13. By paragraph 3 of Martial Law Order No. 132 the following was substituted for paragraph 6 of Martial Law Order No. 103: 

 "An ex-officer of any defence service, whether commissioned, junior commissioned or non-commissioned, appointed on contract in any government post or office or in any local authority at any time after the date of the commencement of Martial Law Order No. 103 dated 25th June, 1985 and before the commencement of this Order and in service on such contract on the date of the commencement of this Order, shall, on the commencement of this Order be deemed to have been absorbed permanently in the service of the Republic or, as the case may be, of the concerned local authority [.]" 

 17. The term absorption can hardly be used with reference to a contract service. For a short time, because of martial law fiats, the term was incongruently made applicable to contract service as well. The appellant's appointment was made long after 9 November, 1986, the date of commencement of Martial Law Order No. 135, and hence, all martial law fiats and manoeuvers, made in Martial Law Order Nos. 103, 132 and 135, for absorbing defence personnel in civil administration will be of no avail to him.
